To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
students tend to focus on geometrical and physical aspects, and that the division strategy appears to be a preferred one when it comes to numerically oriented approaches.
the students’ reasoning about stochastic phenomena is characterized by a variety of strategies, which can be divided in three categories: geometrical, numerical and causal.

(a) Students’ understanding of random phenomena is influenced by the different representations they use to describe and reason about such events, (b) Students’ reasoning about random phenomena is influenced and shaped by their prior knowledge, and (c) Students’ reasoning can be improved by providing a rich learning environment, which enables students to interact with a variety of representations and models.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the students’ ways of reasoning about one-object stochastic phenomena, and how this reasoning is related to different representations and models of chance encounters.
how students reason about chance encounters in a computer-based environment, and how this reasoning is affected by their prior experiences with chance phenomena.
how students reason about random events and how they use ICT to support their reasoning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the students’ reasoning about one-object stochastic phenomena is characterized by a mixture of different strategies and representations.
the students’ reasoning is strongly dependent on the type of representation they have at hand.
students are not always ready to accept that chance phenomena can be described in a purely statistical way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
students’ reasoning in this context is not necessarily restricted to one of the three different models.
the students’ understanding of chance encounters was strongly related to the different ways they were represented in the ICT-environment.

the students in our sample have a tendency to focus on the physical aspects of random events, and we suggest that this is due to a lack of experience with random phenomena in general, and a lack of experience of the numerical models for random phenomena in particular.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to take the students’ different ways of thinking seriously and that we need to develop learning activities that support students in developing their own understanding of random events.
